title: No-Huddle Look Effective, But Not Defining, Against Titans
text:
Leading up to the Pittsburgh Steelers’ game against the Tennessee Titans a week ago as of today, the offense was not making great use of the no-huddle set this season, by any means. By the game records, they only recorded 90 snaps out of the no huddle during the first nine games, which is of course exactly 10 plays per game.
They ran nearly triple their season average of no-huddle plays against the Titans, 28 in all, and many have sought to use this increased usage as a cause, or at least a justification, of the improved offensive play, or simply of Ben Roethlisberger’s improved play.
So was that the case, or was it not? Well, for starters, they certainly opened up the game coming out of the no huddle, as five plays on their opening possession—nearly the entire drive—were designated as having been run out of the no huddle. That includes the final play of the drive, which was a 41-yard touchdown pass to Antonio Brown off of a free play due to an impending defensive offside penalty.
Really, they made use out of it in at least some form or fashion on nearly all of their drives, though they did not do so on their second possession. Of course, they did not manage to do a great deal on offense throughout the remainder of the first half, which included another 12 plays out of the no huddle.
The offense only ran 11 plays out of the no huddle in the second half, when they did the majority of their scoring, however, and none of Roethlisberger’s second-half touchdowns were thrown out of it.
Not that it was not an effective package. Overall, the Steelers averaged 6.3 yards per play out of the no huddle against the Titans, while they barely averaged over four yards per play on their 45 additional snaps in the game, excluding kneeldowns.
That does, however, include penalties, including a 15-yard facemask penalty against Marcus Gilbert, as well as a false start on David DeCastro. Removing them does get you to nearly 4.8 yards per play, but that is still a clear disparity from the 6.3 yards out of the no huddle.
One does have to consider the fact that teams don’t run the ball out of the no huddle, as well. There were just three against the Titans, for 11 yards.
Out of the no huddle, Roethlisberger completed only 11 of his 20 pass attempts (also taking a sack), but for 158 yards, averaging 7.9 yards per pass attempt. Outside of the no huddle, he completed 18 of 25 pass attempts, but for 141 yards, averaging 5.6 yards per attempt. But that also includes three touchdowns, one that went for one yard, another for five.
Overall, the no huddle was an effective tool against the Titans, but perhaps not the savior it has been portrayed as. Of course, even no-huddle drives are fluid and occasionally include huddling in select situations, so very little is to be taken in terms of absolutes out of this.
summary: Leading up to the Pittsburgh Steelers’ game against the Tennessee Titans a week ago as of today, the offense was not making great use of the no-huddle set

title: A first? Father, daughter are both members of CIF championships teams
text:
Random thoughts for a Tuesday morning, getting ready for the highly-competitive passing leagues, wondering whatever happened to Nicole Kajitani, the 2006 CIF-SS Division III softball player of the year from Cajon High School.
This could be a first for not only our area, but perhaps Southern California. Of course, incomplete records make it difficult to make such a claim without hesitation.
We have written about fathers and sons who have won football championships as coaches. First there was Bob Baiz reaching the top, including two titles at Claremont High School, followed by son Nick at Rancho Cucamonga. They were followed by Dick Bruich, a CIF champ at Fontana and Kaiser, and son Kurt, the 2014 state champion with Redlands East Valley High School.
Both sons played for their dads on title teams.
Thanks to Yucaipa High School’s 1-0 victory over Mission Viejo in the CIF-SS Division II championship softball game Friday night, we now have a father and daughter who have each won a title.
In 1996, Aaron Alvarado played second base for Rialto High School, which defeated Miller 6-0 for the Division IV crown. It was the second straight title game for coach Scott Russell’s team, which had lost in extra inning to La Quinta.
On Friday night, his daughter Kaitlyn was part of the Yucaipa team that avenged two earlier losses to Mission Viejo, the country’s top-ranked team according to MaxPreps. Kaitlyn is a sophomore and has played third base and pitched.
She has a chance to one-up dad. The final national rankings will come out next week and the T’Birds (31-3) are in good position to finish at No. 1. …
We are always impressed with the mental strength some our of our high school athletes display during trying times.
At the top of the list is Alta Loma High School softball player Cierra Schick, who in a span of days had to deal with tremendous losses.
First, the very unexpected situation of club softball teammate Dana Housley, who died as the result of a ruptured brain aneurysm while on the field. While mourning that loss, her grandfather John Schick passed away, weeks short of his 81st birthday.
Despite losing his eyesight, he was a regular at her games, getting the play-by-play from his son Rich, for years the voice of prep football in the area. Mr. Schick was quite an athlete at Chaffey High School and Chaffey College, where he played football and baseball. He played football briefly at Utah State, serving as a backup for Hall of Famer Merlin Olson.
“He was the smartest man I’ve ever known,” said his son. “As I grew up in this area, I learned quite a bit just following him. Loyalty was one of those lessons.”
The elder Schick formed Fabco Steel in Fontana in 1979. More than 20 years later, his son took over and has been in charge for 22 years. …
From the e-mail box: “Great article about two courageous individuals (Nancy Brown and Ron Reclusado), and two supportive families. Some are asking if the impact of coaches, and the lessons which sports teach are still relevant?
“Look no further!” – B.P., Rancho Cucamonga
We appreciate the kind words. However, enough can’t be said about Nancy Brown and her laser-focused drive to help Reclusado by donating a kidney. All tests have been completed and pass and the procedure is still on schedule for Friday morning.
It is an excellent example of how coaches impact the lives of their students. …
Here’s a big cheer for the Chino High School Sports Boosters, who have opted to honor the school’s past with the present.
Longtime cross-country and track coach John Aguilera has been selected to receive the first Frank M. Elder Award. Elder was an iconic coach in the district and was a very successful one. As such, the award is named for him as the organization honors “legendary coaches who have committed and dedicated their lives to the Chino community and the student-athletes at Chino High School.”
Aguilera was a unanimous choice, thanks to his serving more than 30 years in the community. He had an impact on those who worked for him and those associated with him. …
Can you believe the irony of the horse racing situation in Southern California? First, it’s iconic Hollywood Park grandstands demolished in the same fashion as an old Las Vegas casino. It was a sad sight, despite those claiming victory that the Rams will move it. My last Hollywood bet is that will never happen.
Days later, American Pharoah becomes just the 12th Triple Crown winner, and the first since Affirmed in 1978, with the entire world watching. Perhaps it’s wishful thinking, but wouldn’t it be great if this horse could change the attitude of the public toward the sport.
Here’s a thought: Wouldn’t it have been great if American Pharoah would have been paraded around the Fairplex in September for local fans to cheer, just like other legendary California horses? Oh, that’s right. Fairplex no longer has a horse meet. …
We shouldn’t have been quite so quick in writing off the Los Angeles D-Fenders from playing more games at Citizens Business Bank Arena. Granted the parent team, the Lakers, is considering building a new gym for the developmental squad in El Segundo, but would it be ready for the 2015-16 season?
Actually, the Lakers and arena officials will be meeting this week to discuss as many as six games in Ontario for the 2015-16 campaign. This past season, the team played three games at The Bank, and each contested attracted at least 1,500 people.
That’s twice as many as the new facility will hold. …
Triple Crown, part 2: Do the TV executives have restricted vision, especially when it comes to auto racing. Specifically, the Verizon IndyCar Series.
NBCSN televised the Texas race Saturday night, just hours after American Pharoah won the Triple Crown. It would have been spectacular if the network noted only Juan Pablo Montoya was in position to win the IndyCar Triple Crown following his triumph at the Indianapolis 500.
Only Al Unser has achieved the feat, which in those days included a 500-mile race at Ontario Motor Speedway in addition to event at Indy and Pocono.
Such a mention/graphic might have aided Auto Club Speedway in selling tickets for the June 27 MAV TV 500, to be televised on NBCSN, the second leg of the IndyCar Triple Crown. There’s no question ACS needs the help to promote what will be a great race, but one that has had four different dates in four years.
A Saturday race, starting at 1 p.m., on a different date. Does IndyCar really want this race to succeed?
authors: Nhra Events Since Has Also Staffed High School Football
Since Has Won Several National Awards In Writing

title: How Hard Would It Be to Change the Face on the $20?
text:
On paper, it doesn’t look like it would be difficult to change the faces that greet us on dollar bills whenever we pull out our wallets. The Treasury Secretary has unilateral authority to banish Franklin from the $100 or Lincoln from the five spot whenever he wants; Congress also has the power to change the portraits used on U.S. currency. The possibilities for new monetary muses are nearly limitless — the only requirement is that they be dead, just like the luminaries chosen for stamps. There’s also an expectation that the portraits will be familiar faces from history.
However, the process must be harder than it looks, because the Treasury hasn’t retired a portrait since 1929, when Andrew Jackson replaced Grover Cleveland — which has everyone wondering what will happen with a new campaign to get a woman on the $20.
Plenty of people have tried to change a portrait. Most of these attempts involved Ronald Reagan. In 2004, Grover Norquist tried to boot Alexander Hamilton from the $10 and replace him with the conservative icon; Senator Mitch McConnell thought the idea was a great one. “Hamilton was a nice guy and everything, but he wasn’t president,” Norquist told USA Today. At the same time, a few House Republicans were trying to get Reagan put on the $20. Six years after those efforts failed, Representative Patrick McHenry sponsored legislation to get Reagan on the $50.
“There’s an inherent conservatism when it comes to money here,” notes Matthew Wittmann, assistant curator of American coins and currency at the American Numismatic Society.
A new group has decided to try a different tack by advancing a new portrait that is not Ronald Reagan. Women on 20s has started a campaign to get a woman on money that Americans use (unlike $1 coins) — something that even President Obama has said is a “pretty good idea.” They’ve even picked the perfect guy to kick off currency — Andrew Jackson, once best known for military prowess, and now remembered for causing the Trail of Tears.
“Andrew Jackson folks would complain,” says Daniel Feller, an expert on our seventh president at the University of Tennessee at Knoxville, “but there aren’t many Andrew Jackson folks left. I don’t know who in government would be against it.”
However, the problem was never going to be complaints about keeping Jackson on the $20; it was always going to be about narrowing the entire universe of eligible women to put on the bill to one in a town where agreeing is often a laughable dream, and everyone has different reasons for wanting to try something new with currency — or keep it the same.
When the Treasury thinks about redesigning money, it isn’t about the politics. The department — along with the Federal Reserve, the Secret Service, and the Bureau of Engraving and Printing — is always thinking about how to best stop people from counterfeiting it. (Everyone forgets, but the Secret Service was created to protect money, not the president.) That’s why dollar bills have slowly morphed over time, with stripes and nearly unnoticed whizbangs continually cluttering the currency, and the important men in them shifting in their invisible seats and switching up their stare. A Treasury official, who stressed the department’s aim to prevent unauthorized production of money, was unable to talk about any specific campaigns to change currency design “or about anything political.”
Other groups have successfully lobbied to change other parts of dollar bills recently, but it took lots of money or a winning court case. The D.C. District Court decided in 2008 that the Treasury must “take such steps as may be required to provide meaningful access to United States currency for blind and other visually impaired persons,” siding with the American Council of the Blind. Designing a new bill can take a long time; seven years after the court case, the Treasury knows that the $10 will be the first bill with tactile features, but they’re still working on making sure the design in super counterfeit-proof. The $1, on the other hand, has managed to avoid redesign for more than 75 years, thanks in part to the efforts of the National Automatic Merchandising Association — the vending-machine lobby. If the $1 bill were redesigned, all vending machines currently handing out Mountain Dews to the masses would need to be redesigned as well. The Treasury isn’t too worried about the $1 bill being counterfeited, either. So George stays the same, the Dorian Gray of the dollar bills.
Women on 20s wanted to avoid getting into politics — especially Congress, according to Susan Ades Stone, executive director of the campaign. They didn’t want to create a new denomination, because that would require congressional approval. They didn’t want to try to get a revolving series of women on a bill, because that would likely trigger a review process. They wanted to pick something within the Treasury’s budget, and don’t plan to approach the department with their plan until their supporters have narrowed down the list of 15 portrait candidates to one. More than 180,000 people have voted, and it’s hard to find a publication that hasn’t written about the idea.
“With the environment in Washington, we wanted to do something as realistic and nonpolitical as possible,” Stone said. Even if Women on 20s tries to eliminate all politics from the process, it’s easy to see how Washington could inject it back in. Everyone won’t agree on the woman chosen to replace Andrew Jackson. Margaret Sanger, who helped popularize birth control, is one of the women being voted on in Women on 20s online poll. You can imagine the Treasury being hesitant to court the inevitable controversy that would come with her being named as the face of the $20. Other women in the running include Betty Friedan, Sojourner Truth, Rachel Carson, and Rosa Parks — all important, some equally bound to cause political tantrums. Wittmann has offered Amelia Earhart as the ideal portrait, citing her popularity and apolitical place in memory.
Even if the apolitical ideal could be chosen, it’s impossible to imagine that Congress would allow the Treasury to make such an big change without their input. The Treasury would probably want to defer to Congress in these matters anyway, unless they learned that putting a woman on the $20 was the best way to repel counterfeiters. At that point, a million different lobbies and groups’ desires would begin mingling with lawmakers’ own biases and hopes in choosing the first woman to appear on a dollar, and everyone would remember why nothing has changed since 1929. Knowing Congress, this debate could descend into another failed attempt to get Reagan immortalized on a bank note.
However, hundreds of thousands of people pushing for change is no small thing. Wittman is “cautiously optimistic” about the campaign. “It seems a little bit strange,” he says, noting that Australia puts a woman and man on every denomination of paper currency, “it seems a little bit backwards that the United States can’t find someone to honor beyond this small subset of founding fathers and dead presidents.”
Stone says that Women on 20s has “already succeeded” by getting people to talk about the famous women she would like to honor. “We’ve done exactly what we aimed to do — get a lot of people thinking.” Feller, the Andrew Jackson scholar, is also pleased that people are talking about this issue, although for different reasons. “I get to talk more to newspaper people who don’t care about what I think about the 1830s.”
summary: The Treasury hasn't subbed out a portrait on a dollar bill since 1929.

title: Arsenal Legend Rates Thibaut Courtois And Hugo Lloris As ‘Outstanding’
text:
View image | gettyimages.com
Arsenal have been chopping and changing their goalkeepers this season and a legendary club figure thinks that they are badly lagging behind local rivals Spurs and Chelsea between the posts.
Bob Wilson was the Arsenal keeper when they won the double in 1971 spoke to the Evening Standard about the goalies at his former club and the players he really rates in that position.
"The goalkeepers that we have there at the moment are really good solid goalkeepers but then you've got to look right across the board and there are two goalkeepers this year that haven been truly outstanding.
"The two who stand out are obviously Thibaut Courtois at Chelsea and Hugo Lloris at Tottenham has just been absolutely amazing.”
It’s a sad fact for Arsenal fans to accept but it would cost them an absolute fortune to buy a keeper anywhere near as good as Courtois or Lloris. Has Arsene Wenger still got it in him to unearth a bargain in the transfer market?

title: Gov. Perdue: Herbalife to create 493 jobs in Winston-Salem
text:
Please enable Javascript to watch this video
WINSTON-SALEM, N.C. -- Gov. Perdue announced Wednesday Herbalife will make the former Dell plant in Winston-Salem its new East Coast manufacturing facility, creating nearly 500 jobs.
"Herbalife you are going to be glad you picked this community to live and work in." she proclaimed.
The vitamin and weight loss supplement company promises to invest $106.5 million and create 493 local full-time jobs over the next three years in exchange for $13.9 million in state and local incentives.
Local economic leaders were able to beat out officials in Gwinnett County, Georgia, who were also trying to lure Herbalife, thanks mainly to a vacant state-of-the-art 750,000-square-foot facility open and ready.
“It's nice that they don't have to construct, – it's already there,” said Margaret Crowley who lives near the plant and remembers the hope it brought when it was first built.
“We went through all the construction on the road and the big plans, – very excited and then it fizzled out.”
The failure of Dell to keep operating the facility, after being handed millions in taxpayer incentives, leaves many local residents skeptical of new companies and local leaders negotiating more incentives deals.
Dell paid back the incentives due when it failed to stay open.
"I really hope they are here to stay," said Winston-Salem resident Sandra Williams who had a member of her family get laid off when Dell left town.
“They bought a house, bought two cars and then the rug is pulled out ... still at Forsyth Tech trying to find a job.”
The new jobs are expected to pay around 40,000 thousand dollars a year.
Herbalife hopes to be up and running by June 2014.

title: France Asked to Prolong Stay of Refugees in Beirut; 700 Danzig Exiles Survive 4-month Odyssey
text:
Leading French Jewish relief organizations appealed to the Foreign Ministry today for at least a one-month extension of the temporary permit under which 658 refugees, including two American citizens and 28 non-Jews, are staying in Beirut, Syria.
Should the Appel be rejected, the refugees, who were quarantined in Beirut when the freighter Frossula was hit by an epidemic at sea, face immediate re-embarkation and resumption of their three-month odyssey in search of a haven.
Meanwhile, details were received here of the inhuman experiences undergone by about 700 Danzig refugees who drifted for four months on the Mediterranean before being dumped on the shores of Palestine. Without passports, the refugees embarked on their voyage on an old freighter equipped with a supply of food and water calculated to last three weeks. Despite rationing of a bowl of potato soup and a slice of sausage for an entire day, the food and water supply was exhausted in a month.
Parched and hungry, the passengers were forced to seek food by approaching the Greek shore, where local Jews delivered aboard ship a limited quantity of food. The entire supply, however, was seized by the freighter’s crew, who refused to feed anyone unless paid with money, valuables or even articles of clothing.
The crew, completely out of hand, robbed the passengers of all their valuables and then forced those with relatives in America and Palestine to cable for money to be sent to a bank on a Greek island. The money was delivered to the ship and confiscated by the crew.
The ship’s captain, who displayed sympathy for the passengers and tried to maintain discipline, was forcibly replaced by two sailors who took over command of the vessel. The saga of piracy and suffering on the high seas was ended for the refugees when they were finally dumped, the women clad only in bathing suits and the men in pajamas, on the shores of Palestine.

title: Beware of dishonest building contractors
text:
Just ask the folks at Hugo City Hall: Unscrupulous contractors are out there.
On Tuesday, city officials denied several contractors who applied for credentials to do business in tornado-hit neighborhoods, said City Administrator Mike Ericson.
The contractors did not meet the city’s minimum standards for doing business in the “hot zone,” he said.
“Natural disasters bring out individuals who want to prey on victims who really need honest, reputable contractors,” Ericson said.
City officials warned residents to use caution before hiring anyone to do work.
Bryan Bear, the city’s community development director, said residents should not trust contractors who arrive in unmarked vehicles, offer extremely low prices or refuse to provide written estimates.
Homeowners should thoroughly check out anyone they hire, or they could end up having shoddy work done, paying too much or having someone run off with their money, said Doug Neville, information officer with the Minnesota Department of Public Safety.
“Whenever there is a disaster, we know that, within days, there’s going to be a group of people who will attempt to take advantage of homeowners,” said Barb Grieman, vice president of the Better Business Bureau of Minnesota and North Dakota.
So if you’ve got a mess from the storm, here’s advice from the Better Business Bureau and Minnesota Department of Labor and Industry:
If you think insurance may cover the repairs, call your agent or company to get an adjuster out to your home to get a damage evaluation, an itemized repair list and a repair cost estimate. Save all your receipts.
Be skeptical of anyone who comes to your door to offer services, wants to be paid in cash or insists you sign a contract before having a chance to check out the company.
Research the company’s reputation before hiring. Contact the Better Business Bureau at 651-699-1111 or www.thefirstbbb.org.
Ask for proof of liability and workers’ compensation insurance; make sure it is current.
Don’t rely on verbal promises — make sure they’re written in the contract. Materials and completion dates should be in there, too.
Don’t sign anything you don’t fully understand, and read the small print carefully.
Don’t make the last payment until the work is done and you are satisfied with it.
If you have a complaint about work that was done, call the Better Business Bureau or contact the Minnesota Attorney General’s Office at 651-296-3353 or www.ag.state.mn.us. Both entities can try to contact the company and ask it to do the job to your satisfaction.

title: Cool Spaces: Farm transforms into chic country venue (PHOTOS)
text:
Right now, it's a beehive of activity.
Workers of every skill level are feverishly laboring to transform Bell Gate Farm's barn into a premier wedding and event venue.
Located in Lower Milford Township, Lehigh County, Bell Gate is a 268-acre working farm that has been owned by the Stevens family since 1985.
The barn itself is actually two floors. The top floor will be known as the Great Barn and will be suitable for events of up to 200 people. The bottom floor is the Prohibition Room and its target is smaller events.
It is all the brainchild of Stephanie Stevens, who inherited the property from her late parents. Stevens lives on the property with her daughter but knew she had to come up with a revenue stream to be able to keep it in the family.
Cool Spaces: Country charm at old farmhouse
A bed and breakfast was one idea but she quickly scrapped that when she realized just how many hurdles one had to jump through for it. With her events-planning background - she spent years working for large companies planning major events - the idea was born to use the existing barn to create a really cool space for weddings and other events.
With two main goals -- to maintain the architectural integrity of the buildings while keeping the working part of the farm for farming, and to create a place for the community to enjoy -- she began to transform the property.
All of that meant that she had to come up with some pretty creative uses of things like existing silos, a bullpen and a pond. With the help of landscapers, and a creative team, she has a vision that in time will include water features, extensive landscaping and fire pits.
For now, though, she's working on getting the Great Room and Prohibition Room ready.
She also wanted to make sure she created a space that brides and others would find beautiful but affordable. With that in mind, and with her experience as a planner, she is offering full service including lighting, decor, food and planning services.
With her first booked event in just a couple of weeks, it looks like there is an insurmountable amount of work to be done, but she's not worried. In fact, she said, she is confident Bell Gate Farm will be ready to go.
Stevens also has a vision that will take her well beyond weddings and events, including using the property to create a Longwood Gardens-type destination and to host community events.
Bell Gate Farm is located at 7081 Bell Gate Road, just off the Limeport Pike, in Lower Milford Township. For information, visit bellgatefarm.com.
Do you know of any cool spaces that you'd like to share? Let us know by leaving a comment below or email me at kjfrantz@lehighvalleylive.com. Follow lehighvalleylive.com on Twitter at @lehighvalley. Find lehighvalleylive.com on Facebook.
summary: Bell Gate Farm is undergoing a transformation as its owner gets it ready for its next purpose: a full-service events venue.

title: New York Times Company introduces self-serve local ads on its blogs
text:
In a post on The Local, a three-month-old New York Times blog targeted to the historic-meets-hip-hop Fort Greene and Clinton Hill neighborhoods of Brooklyn, editor Jim Schachter explained the site’s new “hyperlocal” ads that advertisers can set up themselves. The beginning CPM (“cost per mille,” the price for 1,000 impressions) is $5, which means that five bucks gets your ad shown to a thousand people.
The Local is going after plumbers and pizza parlors, hoping they’ll choose the site over Google, Craigslist or other ads not pegged to a neighborhood publication. “The idea is to create an affordable place to advertise local businesses, restaurants, services and events,” Schachter said.
The New York Times Company is looking for revenue everywhere, after suffering continually dwindling ad income and continually dwindling profits for the past few years. A big part of The Local’s design is that compared to The New York Times’ flagship newspaper, it’s an informal, colloquial blog. That could prove to be a good wrapper for neighborhoody ads that aren’t overly slick. In ways such as this, the Times seems to be trying to invent its own competition.
(Disclosure: Paul Boutin is a freelance contributor to the Times.)

title: Quebec lumber workers among first hit by duty-inspired layoffs
text:
By Ross Marowits
Hundreds of Quebec forestry workers are experiencing the first sour tastes from the softwood lumber battle with the United States as they prepare for the start of layoffs.
Starting Monday, Resolute Forest Products is cutting shifts at seven sawmills and delaying the start of forest operations that will affect 1,282 workers.
Pierrot Fortin, who experienced such heartache during the last impasse in the early 2000s, is again preparing for lost income and uncertainty.
“Work stoppages like this are never easy,” said the truck driver who hauls wood from forests in the Lac-St-Jean region.
“It has an impact on families and everyone is worried.”
But the 48-year-old says he’s luckier than some — his house is almost paid off and his two children are no longer babies.
Fortin feels for young families and older workers who have few employment alternatives in one-industry towns.
The big worry is temporary curtailments will be extended as companies feel growing pressure from retroactive duties and the prospect of additional preliminary charges to be announced next month.
During the last softwood lumber dispute, Canada shed 20,000 forestry jobs between 2000 and 2006, and about 400 sawmills closed entirely between 2004 and 2009.
Unifor, which represents 24,000 forestry workers at 134 companies, fears duties this time will hurt 25,000 Canadian jobs.
La Tuque Mayor Normand Beaudoin says any downtime longer than two weeks currently planned for about 100 mill employees would be difficult for families in the small town about 200 kilometres south of the Lac-St-Jean region.
“In the short-term, I don’t have a lot of worries, but if it goes on for one or two years it will do a lot of harm,” Beaudoin said.
Although workers were aware of the challenges facing the industry, they were surprised by the speed with which Resolute moved to cut costs — especially since the company’s preliminary duties are below the 20 per cent Canadian average with no retroactivity, said Daniel Leblond, president of the Unifor local at the Dolbeau-Mistassini sawmill.
Resolute said the immediate effect on the industry is largely because of volatility in market pricing, thanks to the duties, and the fact some U.S. customers had built up some supply in anticipation of the duties.
Still, it has created anxiety because there are no answers to questions if the layoffs will be extended.
“These families are devastated, just like if they were struck by a hurricane,” said Leblond.
He fears more job cuts are coming at two paper mills if there’s no relief from punishing duties on supercalendered paper.
The Quebec mills are among the first in Canada to feel the effects of softwood duties. However, a cedar mill in New Brunswick recently closed, affecting six workers.
Danny Stillwell, owner of Hainesville Sawmill Ltd., northwest of Fredericton, said he’s closing for at least six months until a dispute over the new tariffs is resolved.
There’s no word of any mill closings in Western Canada, but workers are nervous, said Bob Matters, wood council chairman for the United Steelworkers union.
“Many of the workers, probably most of them, have been through the last round of softwood lumber negotiations, and the uncertainty around how long this will last is what is causing the grief,” he said.
With many families having several members employed in the forest sector, Matters added, any cuts cause widespread pain and have far-reaching ramifications for forest-dependent communities.
“The major employer in town is the mill or manufacturing facility so it is a very big deal.”
Meanwhile, the Union des municipalités du Québec were in Washington on Saturday to lobby for support of a softwood lumber deal between Canada and the United States. The UMQ delegation, headed by Drummondville Mayor Alexandre Cusson, is expected to make a statement Tuesday on the mission.
Presse Canadienne contributed to this report
summary: Starting Monday, Resolute Forest Products is cutting shifts at seven sawmills and delaying the start of forest operations that will affect 1,282 workers.

title: How good is Kentucky's pitching this year? 'At a minimum ... the best staff in the SEC'
text:
LEXINGTON, Ky. – It’s not every season the reigning pitcher of the year in college baseball’s preeminent conference is not even guaranteed to retain his spot as the staff’s ace.
But that’s exactly where junior right-handed pitcher Sean Hjelle found himself on a Kentucky staff with at least four pitchers who could be early-round draft picks in the next two years.
“I’m convinced that at a minimum we’re going to be the best staff in the SEC,” Hjelle said. “We should for sure be a top-five pitching staff in the country. The talent on this pitching staff, and the team as a whole, is unmatched. I’m very confident in this entire team, but especially our pitching staff.”
Making players earn their spots on a team, regardless of previous performance, is nothing new in coaching, but UK boasts the talent and depth on its pitching staff to make coach Nick Mingione’s challenge to Hjelle hold weight.
Junior right-handed pitcher Justin Lewis turned down the chance to sign with the Tampa Bay Rays as the team’s 11th-round pick in order to return to school and has added a slider to his pitching arsenal in the offseason. Sophomore Zack Thompson, who Baseball America ranks as the Southeastern Conference’s best prospect for the 2019 draft, was one of the stars of UK’s NCAA Tournament regional win last season and a 2017 Freshman All-American.
Senior Brad Schaenzer, who won all five of his decisions as a mid-week starter and reliever last season, returns. Junior-college transfer Zach Haake, Baseball America’s No. 75-ranked prospect for the 2018 draft, will likely fill a similar role after returning from a hand injury.
“When you look at the teams that have competed for national championships, that’s what they’re throwing,” Mingione said. “They’re throwing seven to 10 guys, and those are the guys that are chewing up the bulk of the innings. This has good depth. How Zach Haake comes back from the injury and how he does is obviously going to be a key piece, but there’s definitely some talent and depth there, and one that I believe gives us a chance to make a run to win the whole thing.”
MORE: Could Cats be headed to first College World Series? Get to know the 2018 UK baseball team
MORE: 2017 NCAA super regional | Season ends for ‘really amazing’ Kentucky baseball team
After losing three of its top four hitters from the 2017 super regional team, UK may need its pitching staff to carry the load early while a group of unproven hitters, including at least three junior-college transfers who will likely start in the opening day lineup, adjust to expanded roles.
But the pitching depth and talent should also allow Mingione to emphasize defense in his lineup, knowing that the Wildcats could score fewer runs in 2018 but still win more games.
Mingione and his staff looked at the SEC’s defensive statistics from recent seasons to determine UK needs to commit 16 fewer errors in 2018 if it is to rank among the “elite” teams in the league.
“We cut out those 16 errors, we win the super regional, we go to Omaha, we win Omaha,” Hjelle said. “… This game comes down to little things and inches every single day. Cutting out 16 errors is huge for us, and that’s what’s going to get us to Omaha.”
A strikeout-heavy pitching staff — the three weekend starters combined to average just less than a strikeout per inning pitched last season — should go a long way to limiting the opportunity for defensive miscues.
“Say we strike out 10, well, there’s 17 (outs left),” Mingione said. “If we can get them to hit four routine fly balls, now we only need 13. … It’s like the amount of plays you have to make become less and less and less because you have a pitching staff that can strike guys out, which we’ve proven that we could do last year. …
“So anytime you do that, yes, there will be times where our lineup will not be based on just what you can do offensively but defensively because we understand the importance of it.”
Hjelle answered Mingione’s challenge to earn back his spot as the Wildcats’ Friday starter. He proved capable of putting the entire team on his back in the NCAA regional last season when he won the opener then recorded the final 10 outs of the series-clinching victory three days later.
Now Hjelle appears to have more than enough help to lead Kentucky to an even longer run in postseason play.
“Our hitting is going to come around, our hitting is going to be fine,” Lewis said. “I think when we put those two together we’ll be a very tough team to stop.”

title: Convicted killer wanted by Calgary police
text:
Calgary police are looking for a convicted killer who removed a court-ordered tracking device before a daily curfew check with authorities.
Kevin Ronald Brooks, 28, was released from prison in June, after serving every day of a seven-year manslaughter sentence behind bars. Because authorities consider Brooks a high risk to reoffend, they issued a public warning about his release and obtained a court order requiring him to wear an electronic ankle bracelet and submit to daily curfew checks.
However, officers who went to check on Brooks early Friday were greeted by an alarm that sounds when the ankle bracelet is removed.
Brooks’ manslaughter conviction stems from the April 2007 shooting death of Kevin Palmer in Saint John, N.B. The two men were sitting in a car in a city park when Brooks shot Palmer, 29, with a sawed-off shotgun he said he carried for protection due to a drug debt he owed.
Police said Brooks has a history of violent offences committed in Edmonton and Drumheller as well.
Brooks is Caucasian, six feet tall and approximately 160 pounds. He has brown hair, brown eyes and multiple tattoos — including one around his neck and teardrops by the corner of his right eye.
